title: Faber withdrawing Sally Rooney's books from the UK is no overreaction
gist: Faber has stopped supplying Sally Rooney's books in the UK because Section 15 of the Terrorism Act 2000 could criminalise paying her royalties, given she says she will fund the proscribed Palestine Action. The author argues the legal reading is sound and that UK terrorism law has been discredited by a 1,553% jump in terrorism-related arrests.

insights.claim: Faber has withdrawn Sally Rooney's books from UK supply in all formats because current legislation prevents it from passing UK earnings to her.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Shows proscription law reaching into mainstream commercial activity; watch for other publishers and authors facing similar exposure.

insights.claim: Section 15 of the Terrorism Act 2000 criminalises receiving or providing money that one knows or has reasonable cause to suspect will be used for terrorism, which would cover taking and paying out royalties.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Defines the legal channel through which a proscription creates financial-flow liability for companies.

insights.claim: Because Rooney publicly said she intends to use her royalties to fund Palestine Action, the elements of the Section 15 offence appear made out for both her and her publisher, so their reading of the law is not fanciful.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Compliance counsel at publishers and payment intermediaries may treat statements of intent as knowledge triggers.
insights.quote: There is a risk of criminal liability.
insights.locator: Rooney, in turn, has said openly

insights.claim: Withdrawing books runs against both parties' commercial interests, so Faber agreeing to it implies it sees credible legal liability rather than staging a publicity stunt.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A costly self-imposed commercial sacrifice is a signal of perceived legal risk, not PR.
insights.locator: Indeed, it is against the commercial interests

insights.claim: UK Home Office statistics show 3,867 terrorism-related arrests in the year to June 2026, up from 234 the prior year, a 1,553% rise and 1,525% above the 10-year median of 238.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A step-change in arrest volumes signals aggressive enforcement of the Palestine Action ban and potential strain on policing and courts.
insights.locator: Last week the Home Office published the statistics

insights.claim: The author contends the surge in arrests consists mainly of people holding placards supporting Palestine Action, making terrorism law look unserious.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Expect continued political and legal pressure on the proscription, which affects civil-liberties and reputational risk for the government.

insights.claim: The author calls the proscription of Palestine Action, a direct-action protest group, as a terrorist organisation a ludicrous decision by then home secretary Yvette Cooper and the Home Office.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Marks the proscription as a contested policy likely to stay in the headlines.
insights.locator: But little about the terrorism law

insights.claim: The High Court held the Palestine Action ban disproportionate and unlawful, but a higher court on government appeal held it proportionate and lawful, and the Supreme Court hears the latest appeal next month.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The November Supreme Court hearing is the key near-term catalyst for whether the ban and its commercial knock-ons persist.
insights.locator: The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom will next month

insights.claim: The author expects the Supreme Court, which defers to government on national security and political judgement, is unlikely to overturn the ban.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Base case is that the proscription and related exposure remain in force.
insights.quote: The Supreme Court as currently constituted is deferent to the government
insights.locator: But maybe this proscription is too much
